FoldAgent: Agent-Assisted Logic Folding with Automated Verification

Openly licensed edition · 31 October 2026
Zhanchen Zhao, Wenyu Sun, Yaqing Lai, Yubo Deng
Tsinghua University (all authors)
Conference representative: Zhanchen Zhao.

An agent-assisted SKY130 design case: generate partitioned RTL, check the service contract automatically, and follow physical feedback to closure.

Reading route: choose the cut → predict the connection budget → understand the local repair → trace the round trip. Use the timing window to interpret arrival margins.

Abstract

FoldAgent connects agent-assisted RTL partitioning to automated circuit checks in a worked two-tier INT8 design. With projected footprint fixed at 1 mm² and a second 1 mm² logic tier added, this signed INT8 design case preserves cycle-level supply and completion throughput across 162 paired scenarios. To retain the original schedule, its chosen cut uses 725 functional cross-tier connections and a same-cycle control → compute → storage round trip.

Preserving that schedule creates concrete physical work: protecting fixed endpoints, routing terminal access, managing antenna-diode loading and timing the connected circuit with propagated clocks. We trace these obligations through measured repairs and joint analysis at a 100 ns clock, using a TT library corner and three assumed vertical-RC models. The contribution is a reproducible engineering teaching case connecting a specific service contract to its communication and closure costs, within the stated footprint and interconnect assumptions.

1. Why split the logic?

The starting point is a reduced compute block attached to eight useful memory channels, with two spare interfaces for static repair. Its footprint is constrained to 1 mm². Memory-interface regions, supply structures and vertical connection keepouts consume placement and routing resources inside that footprint. The design must retain its parallel arithmetic and buffering: reducing those resources would change the service delivered by the block.

Logic folding gives these resources a second 1 mm² tier. The projected footprint stays at 1 mm² and total logic silicon becomes 2 mm². This creates a useful engineering question: can we preserve the cycle-level service of the original block while closing the resulting cross-tier circuit? Here, “folding” means a structural partition of one RTL block into two physical logic dies.

Existing work provides open 3D backend flows, including Open3DBench. Bonding-terminal legalization is also an established physical-design problem; Pentapati et al. study width and spacing constraints at these interfaces. Our case combines an explicit memory-service contract, a fixed semantic cut and a source-bound path from functional comparison to two-tier electrical acceptance.

The 1 mm² footprint is an imposed design condition in this case. The comparison establishes preserved service across the chosen split and a two-tier implementation under the stated checks. A fair physical comparison would also close the same-resource single-tier design at 1 mm² and an equal-total-silicon single-tier design at 2 mm² with matching interfaces, clocks and workloads. These baselines, final ECO area and activity-based energy are the next measurements for assessing a stacking advantage.

2. A circuit with an explicit service contract

Each job computes eight signed outputs: Y[j] = Σ X[i] × W[i,j], with j = 0…7 and K = 4, 16 or 64. Inputs and weights are signed 8-bit integers; accumulation uses signed 32-bit values. One tile consumes four input values and an eight-lane weight row, using 32 products. Eight independent memory interfaces may respond at different times. A four-row queue retains partial responses, while input and output ping-pong banks allow overlap between preparation, computation and consumption.

Read by function: blue identifies the control & storage tier; amber identifies the compute tier. Follow the data down to the arithmetic and back up to the output buffer in Figure 1.

The control & storage tier owns configuration, memory requests and responses, the four weight rows, input/output banks, and job/consume control. The compute tier owns all products, reductions and accumulator state. The 352 bytes comprise 128 bytes of inputs, 128 bytes of weight rows, 64 bytes of output banks and 32 bytes of accumulators. Metadata and added physical buffers are accounted separately.

The split preserves the original external protocol. Host pins enter through the compute tier and pass to the control & storage tier; the memory-side ports remain on the control & storage tier. Clock and reset follow explicit physical paths. The last tile returns the combinational next sum to the control & storage tier in the same logical cycle, which preserves the original completion schedule and creates a real round-trip timing path.

Why choose this boundary?

The experiment fixes the arithmetic concurrency, payload capacity, host-facing control location and cycle-level service contract. Within those conditions, this cut keeps the state that coordinates memory responses together and moves each complete arithmetic lane with its accumulator. The following rationale follows the implemented RTL and the fixed contract; alternative partitions are design options for later measurement.

DecisionWhy it fits this circuitPhysical obligation / alternative
Keep the four-row weight queue beside memory controlEight lanes can return independently. The queue retains partial rows; row-valid bits, outstanding requests and consume state jointly decide when all eight lanes are ready. Keeping them together retains one reservation and consumption rule.Send the selected 256-bit weight row to computation. Moving the queue would also require distributing response identity, valid state and reservation ownership across the boundary.
Keep accumulators with the arithmeticEach of eight 32-bit accumulators feeds the next sum on every consumed tile. Placing the state beside its adder keeps the recurrence within the compute tier.Return eight next sums to the output banks. Keeping accumulator state on the control tier would move the recurrence feedback across the boundary and require another timing/traffic design.
Return the 256-bit next sum without another pipeline registerThe last tile writes the output bank at the original completion point. This preserves the existing cycle contract and gives a direct paired comparison.Accept a combinational round trip and verify it with propagated clocks. A registered link could ease a timing segment, while requiring a revised capture schedule, control and buffering; its throughput needs measurement.
Retain host control above package-facing portsThe pilot specification fixes host-facing command/configuration and output ordering on the control tier; package ports enter at the compute tier.Budget 179 host feedthrough bits: 24.7% of all functional connections. Changing this ownership is a separate partition experiment.

This choice spends 725 of 784 functional sites (92.5%) to retain the original service schedule. Its value as a design example is the visible exchange: simple ownership and unchanged cycles create a wide interface and a measurable timing obligation.

Count the physical cut before routing it

Moving all eight output channels requires 290 forward compute bits (32 input bits, 256 weight bits and two controls), 256 return bits and 179 functional host feedthrough bits: 725 functional links. Clock and reset add two more signal terminals. Each functional link uses real SKY130 transmit and receive buffers; their area and pin capacitance enter implementation and timing.

The proxy geometry contains four 200 × 200 µm windows at 10 µm pitch. Of 1,600 candidate positions, 800 are allocated to supply and 16 to utility, leaving 784 functional positions. The selected cut uses about 92.5% of this capacity. The calculation below screens connection count; the implemented and measured case is eight moved channels at 10 µm pitch.

Try a design decision: predict, run, explain

Before running: increase pitch from 10 to 12.5 µm while keeping the four windows and supply/utility allocation rules fixed. Predict whether the original eight-channel cut still fits. If it overflows, would moving only four channels be enough for the connection budget? Write down your prediction, then run the unchanged calculation below.

What stays fixed? The 179 host feedthrough bits, 32 input bits and two controls remain; each moved channel adds 32 weight bits and 32 return bits. The parameter moved_channels counts arithmetic channels moved across the boundary.

Executed Python · cell 2
import math
def connection_budget(pitch_um, moved_channels):
    assert math.isfinite(pitch_um) and pitch_um > 0
    assert isinstance(moved_channels, int) and 1 <= moved_channels <= 8
    slots = 4 * math.floor(200 / pitch_um) ** 2
    available = slots - math.ceil(slots / 2) - 16
    required = 179 + 32 + 2 + 64 * moved_channels
    return {"pitch_um": pitch_um, "channels": moved_channels,
            "available": available, "required": required, "fits": required <= available}

assert connection_budget(10, 8)["available"] == 784
assert connection_budget(10, 8)["required"] == 725
assert connection_budget(12.5, 8)["available"] == 496
assert connection_budget(12.5, 4)["required"] == 469
for pitch, channels in [(10, 8), (12.5, 8), (12.5, 4)]:
    print(connection_budget(pitch, channels))
{'pitch_um': 10, 'channels': 8, 'available': 784, 'required': 725, 'fits': True}
{'pitch_um': 12.5, 'channels': 8, 'available': 496, 'required': 725, 'fits': False}
{'pitch_um': 12.5, 'channels': 4, 'available': 496, 'required': 469, 'fits': True}

After running: explain the design decision

Interface capacity: at 12.5 µm pitch, 496 functional sites remain. The eight-channel cut needs 725, exceeding capacity by 229; moving four channels needs 469 and leaves 27 spare sites.

Compute resources: an eight-channel circuit with only four channels moved would need a location, state ownership and schedule for the other four. Reducing the whole circuit to four channels instead changes its arithmetic concurrency. The count model leaves those implementation decisions open.

Throughput evidence: the measured 162-scenario result belongs to the implemented eight-channel cut at 10 µm pitch. A revised cut needs its own RTL, control/buffering design and the same paired performance check. The four-channel case here is an analytical budget exercise; implementation and performance measurement remain future work.

Your conclusion: name the budget that passed and the design/measurement work still required before selecting the four-channel alternative.

3. Agent assistance, automated checks and physical feedback

The supplied reference RTL and fixed split specification define the design task. The recorded workflow contains a planning-agent session and one RTL implementation attempt. Automated checkers then measure the candidate against the circuit contract. Later electrical closure combines tool reports, targeted backend edits and an isolated tool repair, under the documented author approvals.

4. Does folding preserve the memory-fed computation?

The performance comparison uses identical fixed stimulus schedules for the reference and two-tier design. Its 162 scenarios are the Cartesian product of three K values, three repair mappings, three random seeds, three service-delay profiles and two output-backpressure settings. Each scenario measures 1,000 steady completion/service intervals after 100 warmup jobs. We compare cases by their full scenario key, retaining the useful-byte count and both measured cycle totals.

For a fixed useful-byte count, the supply-throughput ratio is the reference supply-cycle count divided by the two-tier design's count. The completion-throughput ratio uses the same relationship for completed jobs. Fast service accepts requests continuously and responds the next cycle. Jitter uses fixed per-lane request-ready schedules and ordered response delays of 1–7 cycles. Burst service collects up to four rows before releasing responses, with a 16-cycle timeout flush. The stalled output consumer is unavailable for the first three of every eleven cycles. Figure 3 groups the same 162 paired records by these conditions.

Why can the shorter job take longer? Under burst service, K = 4 issues one row request per lane, so a job waits for the 16-cycle timeout that releases a partial batch. K = 16 supplies four row requests per lane and triggers the batch release by occupancy. This service-policy effect yields 20 versus 10 cycles/job in both designs. The response model, rather than arithmetic work alone, determines the completion interval here.

All 162 ratios are exactly 1.000. The recorded maximum-latency differences are also zero in every paired scenario. This follows the intended cut: arithmetic concurrency, row buffering and the consume schedule are preserved, with no additional pipeline boundary.

5. What made physical closure difficult?

A successful semantic split still leaves the physical designer with fixed terminals and real loading. Three implementation decisions mattered in this case. Read Figure 4 from conflict to relocation, then Figure 4b for measured coordinates and Figure 2B for the resulting GDS geometry. The 200 × 200 µm cross-tier windows in Figure 2 set connection capacity; the 2.8 µm M4 access window below describes local package-pin access.

Protect the physical interface throughout repair. The endpoint cells keep their identity, location and signal connection. Internal buffering and sizing absorb electrical changes on the logic side. Explicit location/status checks were needed because logical protection alone did not prevent an earlier placement step from moving endpoints; the affected historical candidates remain recorded as invalid.

Treat terminal access as a route. The compute tier package-pin failures concentrated near a constrained bottom-edge strip. A rule-based change increased the internal M4 access window from 2.0 to 2.8 µm while retaining the M5 pin. Local access still required routing around surrounding blocked and supply geometry. The final accepted condition keeps that 2.8 µm window.

Repair antenna loading and geometry together. Added diodes protect routed nets but introduce terminals, capacitance and potential local conflicts. In the final local repair, two newly added diodes moved 8.16 µm upward to sites that meet existing same-net M1 routing. Their old conflicting branches were removed. The scope audit found only one signal route changed in that step; the other 18,205 signal routes and all original port definitions were preserved.

These results support a useful practical rule: after adding electrical fixes, revisit the local route and then recheck the complete design. The last two diode moves illustrate how a small, geometry-driven change can complete closure while retaining the interface and computation.

6. Does the complete circuit meet its timing window?

A receiving register needs a stable input around its clock edge. Setup checks whether the intended value arrives before the latest allowed time. Hold checks whether the next change stays after the earliest allowed time. The distance to each boundary is the timing margin, or slack; a positive value passes that check. Figure 5 first sketches this window, then shows the measured worst margins.

Per-tier implementation uses temporary cross-tier I/O budgets. Joint analysis replaces those internal budgets with actual connected tier netlists, their extracted parasitics and the assumed vertical links. It retains the true external constraints, propagated clock networks and 1 ns uncertainty. Checks include same-tier, control → compute, compute → control and existing round-trip path classes, plus parasitic annotation and constraint coverage.

To test sensitivity to the vertical connection, we use light, nominal and heavy link models. Resistance (R) and capacitance (C) set the modeled interconnect loading; all three use the same typical transistor library. All three joint scenarios pass setup, hold and electrical checks. From the minimum to maximum RC scenario, worst setup slack decreases by about 0.694 ns, from 53.894 to 53.200 ns. Joint worst hold slack stays near 83.600 ps. The local hold check on the compute tier has a 2.448 ps margin with its temporary implementation I/O budgets (25 ns maximum and 0 ns minimum at the internal boundary). Joint analysis removes these internal budgets and times the connected circuit and propagated clock paths, giving a different worst-path population and 83.600 ps worst hold margin. Both checks pass their own constraint sets. Process, voltage and temperature sweeps are the next robustness study; all reported results here use the typical library corner.

Follow the cost of keeping the schedule. Read Figure 6 along the upper arrows first, from launch register to output register; then compare the arrival and deadline in the lower bar. 7. What this case teaches

Budget the whole boundary. Of 725 functional links, 179 carry the host interface. Including this feedthrough is essential when evaluating how much computation fits within the connection windows. The 10 µm proxy geometry leaves 59 functional sites after the chosen cut.

Preserving a schedule creates a physical obligation. Returning the next sum without a new pipeline stage keeps the measured cycle behavior. It also places cross-tier combinational and round-trip paths in the timing graph. Their actual parasitics and clocks have to be evaluated together.

Report the implementation cost alongside the feasibility result. Projected footprint is 1 mm²; total logic silicon is 2 mm². Historical synthesis measured 243,258 µm² for the single-tier reference and 262,841 µm² for the initial two-tier implementation, an approximately 8.1% increase before the later physical ECOs. The final design includes additional clock, buffering and antenna structures. Final activity-based energy and a fully closed equal-silicon comparison are future measurements.

Keep the remaining engineering questions visible. The current evidence covers one physical seed, a TT library corner and three assumed interconnect RC cases. The original RTL-to-GRT SAT proof remains unproved after a stopped diagnostic; backend preservation uses the documented state/connection proofs and simulations. Independent GDS DRC/LVS, calibrated package models, thermal/IR/EM analysis and manufacturing qualification remain future work. Final compute tier ODB/DEF, netlist, SDC and SPEF are frozen. The compute-tier GDS has now been exported directly from that frozen DEF, alongside the reused control-tier GDS. Readback matched per-master instance counts and all physical pin rectangles; see the GDS records. The v5 illustration revision added format export and graphics. This editorial revision reuses those artifacts and all completed experiments.

Start with input binding: from this package directory, run python reproduction/reproduce_performance.py. This regenerates the testbench in memory, reconstructs the nine arithmetic vectors and verifies the RTL, event schedules, checker and complete workload identities against the recorded experiment.

Then, optionally regenerate the central comparison: with Python 3.12 and Icarus Verilog installed, run python reproduction/reproduce_performance.py --run build/paired-reproduction. Choose a new output directory. This compiles both designs and runs 324 simulations with the same stimulus, counts service and completion intervals, saves both new reports and checks all archived metrics. The runner uses four simulation workers and a 600-second timeout per case. The v4 portability validation executed that command in a fresh package extraction and standard-library Python environment with a minimal subprocess environment. All 324 simulations completed and reproduced the archived service cycles, completion cycles, useful bytes and maximum latency values.

That v4 validation used the same host and recorded installed tool binaries; source-build instructions cover obtaining those public versions on another machine. Logs and exact comparisons are included in the portability result.
